paragraphs.text: A loose [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) from 1990, which reaches us through the Guangzhou tea trade. That is the old road for this tea: it went by boat down the river to Wuzhou, on to Guangzhou, and out by sea to the labourers of Southeast Asia who drank it, a route the trade calls the [Nanyang trade](liu-bao:nanyang-trade).

The leaf comes from Cangwu County, near Wuzhou in Guangxi, where the tea takes its name from the town of Liubao. Like every [dark tea](dark:definition), it was piled after it was made, so that warmth, moisture and microbes could turn it darker and softer before it was packed away to age.
At thirty-six years it is far past the ten that the trade sets for [aged Liu Bao](liu-bao:age-aged). Where a lot like this was kept shapes it as much as the years have.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
